summary: PPPoE, as described in RFC 2516, limits the negotiated maximum receive unit to 1492 bytes. This informational memo describes a way to relax that limit so larger values can be negotiated, reducing fragmentation in broadband networks where the underlying links can carry bigger frames.

eli5.summary: Some delivery vans were only allowed to carry small boxes even though the road could handle bigger ones. This lets the vans carry bigger boxes, so fewer things need to be chopped up.

questions: why does pppoe limit packet size to 1492
how can pppoe support jumbo frames
subtitle: How to negotiate larger packet sizes over PPPoE without breaking backward compatibility.

tldr.problem: RFC 2516 limits PPPoE to a maximum receive unit of 1492 bytes, which was appropriate when broadband used Ethernet with ATM, but causes fragmentation in newer designs where the underlying network can carry larger frames (up to 1500 or more).
tldr.mechanism: A new optional tag in the PPPoE discovery phase lets the client tell the server the maximum payload size it can handle. If the server also supports it, both peers negotiate MRU values larger than 1492 following normal PPP rules, and can test the larger size to catch incompatibilities.
tldr.outcome: Networks can use larger frame sizes to reduce fragmentation without breaking compatibility with devices that only support 1492-byte MRU, achieving better efficiency in next-generation broadband.

today: RFC 4638 is an Informational document describing a practical extension to PPPoE. It has not been obsoleted. The extension is widely deployed in broadband networks to reduce fragmentation when Gigabit Ethernet or larger frames are used in the access network.

sections.title: The Problem with Small Packet Sizes
sections.content:
PPPoE (Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet) was designed to carry PPP (the protocol that manages Internet connections) over Ethernet. When PPPoE was standardized in RFC 2516, broadband networks typically linked a customer's PC through an Ethernet cable to a DSL modem (CPE), then over ATM to a DSLAM and BRAS (the broadband network equipment).

In this setup, the customer's PC negotiated a PPPoE session directly with the BRAS. The maximum Ethernet frame is 1500 octets. Since PPPoE adds 6 octets of header and PPP adds 2 octets, that left 1492 octets for the PPP payload. RFC 2516 therefore set 1492 as the maximum negotiated MRU (Maximum Receive Unit) for PPPoE, which made sense at the time.

Modern broadband networks are built differently. They often use Residential Gateways (RGs) that bridge both IP-over-Ethernet and PPPoE sessions, or they support jumbo frames and Gigabit Ethernet. The 1492-byte limit now causes significant fragmentation: larger packets from the customer's network are split into smaller pieces before being transmitted over PPPoE, then reassembled at the other end. This overhead reduces efficiency and performance.
sections.eli5: PPPoE was designed when all frames had to be 1500 bytes. Modern networks can handle bigger frames, but the old 1492-byte limit makes bigger packets get cut up unnecessarily.

sections.title: The Fragmentation Problem in Modern Networks
sections.content:
RFC 4638 describes three problematic network scenarios. In the first, a Residential Gateway bridges between Ethernet (MTU 1500) and PPPoE (MRU 1492), causing fragmentation of packets from the local network when they cross the PPPoE session. In the second scenario, the RG carries both IP-over-Ethernet (IPoE) to the customer and PPPoE to the BRAS, with the same fragmentation problem.

In the third scenario, both PPPoA (PPP over ATM) and PPPoE are involved. A CPE negotiates 1500-byte MRU over PPPoA (a common PPPoA implementation), but when the BRAS strictly complies with RFC 2516 and requires 1492-byte MRU over PPPoE, the BRAS cannot forward 1500-byte packets. Alternatively, if the BRAS accepts 1492 bytes, packets still get fragmented.

The underlying problem is simple: the PPP negotiated packet size limits do not match what the underlying Ethernet frames can carry, leading to unnecessary fragmentation.
sections.eli5: Big packets from the customer need to be chopped into small ones to go through PPPoE, then reassembled on the other side. That's wasteful and slow.

sections.title: The PPP-Max-Payload Tag
sections.content:
The solution is an optional PPP-Max-Payload tag that the PPPoE client can include in the PADI (PPPoE Active Discovery Initiation) and PADR (PPPoE Active Discovery Request) packets during the PPPoE discovery phase. If the server supports larger MRU values, it echoes this tag back in its PADO (Offer) and PADS (Session-confirmation) responses.

The tag has tag type 0x0120, a length of 2 octets, and contains a binary-encoded value representing the maximum PPP payload the client can handle in octets. This value is directly comparable to the PPP MRU negotiation value (unlike the Ethernet frame size, which must account for headers).

By exchanging this information during discovery, both peers know the other's capability before the PPP negotiation phase begins. This allows them to negotiate an appropriate MRU value that both can support.
sections.eli5: During the connection setup handshake, the client tells the server the biggest packet it can handle. If the server agrees, they use that size.

sections.title: Negotiating and Testing the New Size
sections.content:
During the LCP (Link Control Protocol) phase of PPP negotiation, the client and server negotiate an MRU value. If the PPP-Max-Payload tag was exchanged during discovery and its value was greater than 1492, the maximum MRU value that can be negotiated is the minimum of (1) the tag value and (2) the server's interface MTU minus 8 octets (to account for PPPoE and PPP headers).

For backward compatibility, if the PPP-Max-Payload tag is not received or is less than or equal to 1492, the negotiation follows RFC 2516 exactly: the MRU is negotiated normally, but cannot exceed 1492 octets. This preserves compatibility with older implementations that do not support the extension.

Once the session is established with an MRU larger than 1492, the sending side SHOULD optionally test that the receiving side and all intermediate Ethernet equipment can handle packets of that size. It does this by sending one or more Echo-Request packets of the negotiated MRU size. If Echo-Reply packets are received, the path can handle the size. If not, the sender MAY retry with 1492-octet packets, and if those succeed, it MUST limit itself to 1492-octet packets for the session.
sections.eli5: Once both sides agree they can handle bigger packets, one side can test by sending a full-size packet. If it bounces back, they know it works. If it fails, they fall back to the old 1492-byte limit.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Standards
sections.content:
RFC 4638 emphasizes that this solution is informational and does not strictly conform to IEEE standards for Ethernet packet size. The standard Ethernet maximum frame size is 1500 octets. Larger frames (“baby-giants” or “jumbo frames”) are supported by many Ethernet implementations but are not officially standardized by IEEE.

The RFC notes that implementations supporting larger MRU values should exercise caution, as interoperability and reliability cannot be assured. However, backward compatibility is preserved because devices that do not support the PPP-Max-Payload tag will simply not exchange it, and the negotiation will proceed normally with 1492 as the maximum.

The RFC states that both implementors and users should understand that this extension relies on widely deployed behavior of supporting non-standard larger frames, and should test thoroughly before deployment.
sections.eli5: This is not an official IEEE standard, just a practical extension that many networks use. Older equipment ignores the tag and uses 1492 bytes as always, so nothing breaks.
